::: justified-text
[**Gastrointestinal stromal tumors**](https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/rowen.seykora/viz/Mappingbiologicaldiversitywithinararegroupofcancers/Dashboard1 "View data dashboard on Tableau Public") are a class of sarcomas with a shared mesenchymal origin,^1,2^ most commonly arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs), pacemaker cells that help coordinate rhythmic contractions in the gut walls.^3-5^

Sarcoma represents about 1% of adult cancers.^6^ While GIST accounts for anywhere from roughly 14% to 20% of soft tissue sarcoma (STS) cases,^6,7^ it is considered a rare disease, diagnosed in about 10-15 cases per million individuals annually.^2-4^ Since its classification, greater awareness of what drives GIST formation has opened avenues to more effective treatments and improved its prognosis.^3,9^ GIST is heterogeneous across genetic subtype, patient age, and site of tumor origin, among several other factors. Disease management is often interdisciplinary and adjusted to reflect this case-by-case diversity.^10,11^ Genetic subtype is a key focus from diagnosis through treatment, where it predicts initial drug sensitivity and can guide immediate therapeutic course of action.^9-13^ Variables such as patient age and primary tumor site offer diagnostic clues at presentation, assist in risk stratification, and, alongside an understanding of molecular subtype, contribute to overall clinical strategy.^11^ Evaluating individual variation is now a cornerstone of successful GIST management,^3,8^ and this rare cancer stands out as a model of precision medicine in solid tumor treatment.^10-14^
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
icicle = (S) => {
  const h = d3.hierarchy(hierData)
    .sum(d => d.value || 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);

  const root = d3.partition().size([S, S * (h.height + 1) / h.height])(h);
  const offset = root.y1;
  root.each(d => d.target = { x0: d.x0, x1: d.x1, y0: d.y0 - offset, y1: d.y1 - offset });

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, S, S])
    .style("width", `${S}px`).style("max-width", "100%").style("height", "auto")
    .style("overflow", "hidden").style("font", "11px sans-serif");

  const cell = svg.selectAll("g")
    .data(root.descendants().slice(1))
    .join("g")
    .attr("transform", d => `translate(${d.target.y0},${d.target.x0})`);

  const rect = cell.append("rect")
    .attr("width", d => d.target.y1 - d.target.y0)
    .attr("height", d => d.target.x1 - d.target.x0)
    .attr("fill", d => categoryColors.get(d.data.name) ?? colorallx)
    .attr("stroke", colorallx).attr("stroke-width", 1)
    .style("cursor", d => d.children ? "pointer" : "default")
    .on("click", clicked);

  const visible = t => t.y1 <= S + 1 && t.y0 >= -1 && t.x1 - t.x0 > 14;

  const labelText = d => `${d.data.name} (${+d.value.toFixed(1)}%)`;
  const wrapIcicle = function (d) {
    wrapLabel(this, labelText(d), d.target.y1 - d.target.y0 - 8, d.target.x1 - d.target.x0 - 2, { x: 4 });
  };

  const text = cell.append("text")
    .attr("x", 4).attr("y", 12).attr("fill", mutation_color)
    .attr("fill-opacity", d => +visible(d.target))
    .style("pointer-events", "none")
    .each(wrapIcicle);

  cell.append("title").text(tipText);

  let focus = root;
  function clicked(event, p) {
    if (!p.children && p !== focus) return;
    focus = (focus === p) ? p.parent : p;
    const yBase = focus === root ? offset : focus.y0;

    root.each(d => d.target = {
      x0: (d.x0 - focus.x0) / (focus.x1 - focus.x0) * S,
      x1: (d.x1 - focus.x0) / (focus.x1 - focus.x0) * S,
      y0: d.y0 - yBase,
      y1: d.y1 - yBase
    });
text.each(wrapIcicle);
    const t = cell.transition().duration(750)
      .attr("transform", d => `translate(${d.target.y0},${d.target.x0})`);
    rect.transition(t).attr("height", d => d.target.x1 - d.target.x0);
    text.transition(t).attr("fill-opacity", d => +visible(d.target));
  }

  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sunburst = (S) => {
  const h = d3.hierarchy(hierData)
    .sum(d => d.value || 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);

  const levels = h.height + 1;                       // includes the hidden root
  const root = d3.partition().size([2 * Math.PI, levels])(h);
  root.each(d => d.current = d);

  const radius = S / (2 * levels);                   // ring thickness; also the center hole
  const arc = d3.arc()
    .startAngle(d => d.x0).endAngle(d => d.x1)
    .padAngle(d => Math.min((d.x1 - d.x0) / 2, 0.005))
    .padRadius(radius * 1.5)
    .innerRadius(d => d.y0 * radius)
    .outerRadius(d => Math.max(d.y0 * radius, d.y1 * radius - 1));

  const arcVisible = d => d.y1 <= levels && d.y0 >= 1 && d.x1 > d.x0;
  const labelVisible = d => d.y1 <= levels && d.y0 >= 1 && (d.y1 - d.y0) * (d.x1 - d.x0) > 0.03;
  const labelTransform = d => {
    const x = (d.x0 + d.x1) / 2 * 180 / Math.PI;
    const y = (d.y0 + d.y1) / 2 * radius;
    return `rotate(${x - 90}) translate(${y},0) rotate(${x < 180 ? 0 : 180})`;
  };

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [-S / 2, -S / 2, S, S])
    .style("width", `${S}px`).style("max-width", "100%").style("height", "auto")
    .style("font", "9px sans-serif");

  const nodes = root.descendants().slice(1);
  const path = svg.append("g").selectAll("path").data(nodes).join("path")
    .attr("fill", d => categoryColors.get(d.data.name) ?? colorallx)
    .attr("stroke", colorallx).attr("stroke-width", 0.1)
    .attr("d", d => arc(d.current))
    .style("cursor", d => d.children ? "pointer" : "default")
    .on("click", clicked);

  path.append("title").text(tipText);

  // Wrap a label to fit its ring segment (width = ring thickness, height = arc length)
  const wrapRadial = function (d, t = d.current) {
    wrapLabel(this, d.data.name,
      (t.y1 - t.y0) * radius - 8,
      (t.x1 - t.x0) * ((t.y0 + t.y1) / 2) * radius - 2,
      { x: 0, center: true });
  };

  const label = svg.append("g")
    .attr("pointer-events", "none").attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .style("user-select", "none")
    .selectAll("text").data(nodes).join("text")
    .attr("fill", mutation_color)
    .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.current))
    .attr("transform", d => labelTransform(d.current))
    .each(function (d) { wrapRadial.call(this, d); });

  // Center disc: click to zoom back out one level
  const center = svg.append("circle").datum(root)
    .attr("r", radius).attr("fill", "none")
    .attr("pointer-events", "all").style("cursor", "pointer")
    .on("click", clicked);

  function clicked(event, p) {
    if (!p.children) return;
    center.datum(p.parent || root);

    root.each(d => d.target = {
      x0: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x0 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI,
      x1: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (d.x1 - p.x0) / (p.x1 - p.x0))) * 2 * Math.PI,
      y0: Math.max(0, d.y0 - p.depth),
      y1: Math.max(0, d.y1 - p.depth)
    });

    // Re-wrap labels to each section's new size
    label.each(function (d) { wrapRadial.call(this, d, d.target); });

    const t = svg.transition().duration(750);

    path.transition(t)
      .tween("data", d => {
        const i = d3.interpolate(d.current, d.target);
        return k => d.current = i(k);
      })
      .attr("opacity", d => +arcVisible(d.target))
      .attrTween("d", d => () => arc(d.current));

    label.transition(t)
      .attr("fill-opacity", d => +labelVisible(d.target))
      .attrTween("transform", d => () => labelTransform(d.current));
  }
  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wrapLabel = (node, str, maxW, maxH, { x = 0, center = false } = {}) => {
  const cw = 6, lh = 10;                       // approx. char width / line height at 10px font
  const perLine = Math.max(2, Math.floor(maxW / cw));
  const maxLines = Math.max(1, Math.floor(maxH / lh));

  let lines = [], cur = "";
  for (const w of str.split(/\s+/)) {
    const t = cur ? cur + " " + w : w;
    if (!cur || t.length <= perLine) cur = t;
    else { lines.push(cur); cur = w; }
  }
  if (cur) lines.push(cur);

  if (lines.length > maxLines) {
    lines = lines.slice(0, maxLines);
    lines[maxLines - 1] += "…";
  }
  lines = lines.map(l => l.length > perLine ? l.slice(0, perLine - 1) + "…" : l);
  const sel = d3.select(node).text(null);
  const firstDy = center ? 3.5 - (lines.length - 1) * lh / 2 : 0;
  lines.forEach((l, i) =>
    sel.append("tspan").attr("x", x).attr("dy", i === 0 ? firstDy : lh).text(l));
}
```

::: justified-text
**Molecular subtype informs treatment.**^2^ Identification of the oncogene KIT, followed by PDGFRA, as relevant to GIST formation completely changed how clinicians approach its treatment.^1,9,13^ Both encode for receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), surface proteins which help coordinate signals related to cell proliferation and survival.^15^ In healthy cells, this signaling is transmitted in response to relevant biological stimuli.^16^ Activating, or primary, mutations in these genetic drivers elicit ligand- independent activation in the resulting aberrant kinases.^15,17^ Oncogenesis occurs as these signals then persist in the absence of typical molecular cues, driving the unchecked cell proliferation characteristic of GIST neoplasms. ^8,9,18^ The first line of treatment for inoperable cases is often an oral RTK inhibitor, such as Imatinib,^8^ which interacts with some mutant forms of KIT and PDGFRA, slowing cancer progression by dampening abnormal signaling.^18-20^

Activating mutations in KIT or PDGFRA account for 75%-85% of GISTs,^3,4,8,18^ yet roughly 20 primary drivers have been identified.^21-23^ Within the remaining 15%-25% of GISTs, SDH-deficient tumors form a notable subset.^8^ Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) loss of function and subsequent succinate accumulation can drive oncogenesis through broad epigenetic remodeling and pseudohypoxia signaling.^24^ Lastly, SDH-competent, non-KIT/PDGFRA- subtypes may harbor mutations in oncogenes like NF1, BRAF, and RAS, along with NTRK gene fusions.^21,25,26^ For many rarer variants, treatment options are limited; there is an ongoing search for new interventions.^11^

Frequencies of the most common GIST primary mutations are shown in Figure 1. Specific activating mutations can appear in “hotspots” within particular regions of a single driver. Mutations in different exons within one affected gene can modify folding and function of the resulting protein in clinically relevant ways. An oral inhibitor may faithfully bind to one aberrant form of an RTK to restrict cancer growth, yet have no effect on a tumor activated by a different driver.^26^ Imatinib, for example, interacts with key regions of the affected RTK in GISTs with KIT exon 11 and 9 mutations, as well as those with most non-D842V PDGFRA mutations.^19^ On the other hand, PDGFRA D842V mutations occur directly inside the activation loop, impairing binding,^27^ and SDH-deficient GISTs lack these aberrant kinases altogether. As a result, D842V mutation-harboring GISTs are usually unresponsive to Imatinib^9,26^ and SDH deficient GISTS are resistant entirely.^24^ Even within a group of primary tumors with shared activating mutations in KIT, treatment response varies predictably by affected exon.^28^ Cases harboring KIT exon 11 mutations usually exhibit more sensitivity to Imatinib, while those with exon 9 mutations are generally less responsive, and a higher dose is often indicated.^8,10,29^

**Mutational testing helps to anticipate variation in treatment response, allowing care teams to select interventions most likely to yield favorable outcomes.**^20,30^
:::

::: justified-text
**Distributions of molecular subtypes vary by patient age demographic.**^31^ Most older patients have tumors arising from spontaneous mutations in KIT and PDGFRA that develop after decades of life.^32,33^ In pediatric patients, KIT/PDGFRA mutations make up a minority of incidents; familial variants are instead more common.^34^ Inherited drivers such as SDHx, NF1, and familial KIT/PDGFRA mutations result in a predisposition to disease that is present from birth, increasing the odds of tumor growth earlier in life.^35-37^ In this way, age at diagnosis orients diagnostic testing and can streamline treatment selection.^25^ Even after controlling for its association with driver frequencies, age impacts disease management. Guidelines for surgical resection, long-term monitoring, TKI dosing, and risk-adjusted treatment all vary by age group.^38^
:::

Figure 3. Anatomy of GIST Primary Tumor Locations
:::

::: justified-text
GIST can occur throughout the digestive tract, but originates in certain locations more often.^39^ This asymmetry in primary site distribution is clinically relevant. Tumor location of origin has implications for how a case should be managed, and helps predict facets of disease progression, such as probable symptoms and the likelihood of metastasis.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
treemapChart = (W, H) => {
  // Specify the chart’s dimensions.
  const width = W; 
  const height = H;  

  // local stand-in for DOM.uid, bc Quarto doesn't facilitate it
  const prefix = Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8);
  let count = 0;
  const uid = name => {
    const id = `O-${prefix}-${name}-${++count}`;
    return { id, href: new URL(`#${id}`, location) + "", toString() { return `url(${this.href})`; } };
  };

  // This custom tiling function adapts the built-in binary tiling function
  // for the appropriate aspect ratio when the treemap is zoomed-in.
  function tile(node, x0, y0, x1, y1) {
    d3.treemapBinary(node, 0, 0, width, height);
    for (const child of node.children) {
      child.x0 = x0 + child.x0 / width * (x1 - x0);
      child.x1 = x0 + child.x1 / width * (x1 - x0);
      child.y0 = y0 + child.y0 / height * (y1 - y0);
      child.y1 = y0 + child.y1 / height * (y1 - y0);
    }
  }

  // Compute the layout.
  const hierarchy = d3.hierarchy(siteTree) 
    .sum(d => d.value)
    .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value);
  const root = d3.treemap().tile(tile)(hierarchy);

  // Create the scales.
  const x = d3.scaleLinear().rangeRound([0, width]);
  const y = d3.scaleLinear().rangeRound([0, height]);

  // Formatting utilities.
  const format = d3.format(",d");
  const name = d => d.ancestors().reverse().slice(1).map(d => d.data.name).join("→");

  // Create the SVG container.
  const svg = d3.create("svg")
      .attr("viewBox", [0.5, -30.5, width, height + 30])
      .attr("width", width)
      .attr("height", height + 30)
      .attr("style", "max-width: 100%; height: auto;")
      .style("font", "10px sans-serif");

  // Display the root.
  let group = svg.append("g")
      .call(render, root);

  function render(group, root) {
    const node = group
      .selectAll("g")
      .data(root.children.concat(root))
      .join("g");

    node.filter(d => d === root ? d.parent : d.children)
        .attr("cursor", "pointer")
        .on("click", (event, d) => d === root ? zoomout(root) : zoomin(d));

    node.append("title")
        .text(d => `${name(d)}\n${format(d.value)}`);

    node.append("rect")
        .attr("id", d => (d.leafUid = uid("leaf")).id)
.attr("fill", d => {
  if (d === root) return "#c0ecfa";
  let node = d;
  while (node.parent && node.parent.parent) {
    node = node.parent;
  }
  return siteColors.get(node.data.name) || "#ddd";
})
        .attr("stroke", "#fff");

    node.append("clipPath")
        .attr("id", d => (d.clipUid = uid("clip")).id)
      .append("use")
        .attr("xlink:href", d => d.leafUid.href);

    node.append("text")
    .attr("clip-path", d => d.clipUid)
    .attr("fill", d => d === root ? "#000" : "#000")
    .attr("font-weight", d => d === root ? "bold" : null)
      .selectAll("tspan")
.data(d =>
  d === root
    ? [" Click this banner to reset and return to top level."]
    : d.data.name.split(/(?=[A-Z][^A-Z])/g).concat(format(d.value))
)
      .join("tspan")
        .attr("x", 3)
        .attr("y", (d, i, nodes) => `${(i === nodes.length - 1) * 0.3 + 1.1 + i * 0.9}em`)
        .attr("fill-opacity", (d, i, nodes) => i === nodes.length - 1 ? 0.7 : null)
        .attr("font-weight", (d, i, nodes) => i === nodes.length - 1 ? "normal" : null)
        .text(d => d);

    group.call(position, root);
  }

  function position(group, root) {
    group.selectAll("g")
        .attr("transform", d => d === root ? `translate(0,-30)` : `translate(${x(d.x0)},${y(d.y0)})`)
      .select("rect")
        .attr("width", d => d === root ? width : x(d.x1) - x(d.x0))
        .attr("height", d => d === root ? 30 : y(d.y1) - y(d.y0));
  }

  // When zooming in, draw the new nodes on top, and fade them in.
  function zoomin(d) {
    const group0 = group.attr("pointer-events", "none");
    const group1 = group = svg.append("g").call(render, d);

    x.domain([d.x0, d.x1]);
    y.domain([d.y0, d.y1]);

    svg.transition()
        .duration(750)
        .call(t => group0.transition(t).remove()
          .call(position, d.parent))
        .call(t => group1.transition(t)
          .attrTween("opacity", () => d3.interpolate(0, 1))
          .call(position, d));
  }

  // When zooming out, draw the old nodes on top, and fade them out.
  function zoomout(d) {
    const group0 = group.attr("pointer-events", "none");
    const group1 = group = svg.insert("g", "*").call(render, d.parent);

    x.domain([d.parent.x0, d.parent.x1]);
    y.domain([d.parent.y0, d.parent.y1]);

    svg.transition()
        .duration(750)
        .call(t => group0.transition(t).remove()
          .attrTween("opacity", () => d3.interpolate(1, 0))
          .call(position, d))
        .call(t => group1.transition(t)
          .call(position, d.parent));
  }

  return svg.node();
}
```

:::::

::: {style="height: 13px;"}
:::

::: justified-text
Some GISTs (about 15%-47%) are metastatic upon discovery^2^, and primary site may be established through structural and molecular evaluation. Identification of primary site for localized GISTs is comparatively more straightforward. A rare minority of cases present as disseminated GIST, wherein a primary site cannot be determined.^46^ For the majority of cases that can be connected to a single location of origin, tumor site impacts diagnostic workflow and risk stratification. Even after controlling for mitotic rate and tumor size, certain locations are associated with more aggressive disease.^31,41^ Site of origin corresponds with distinct driver mutation frequencies. For example, gastric GISTs present with KIT exon 11 mutations more often, while KIT exon 9 mutations are primarily found in the small intestine.^42,43^ Considering this pattern helps steer diagnostic workflow and predict effective treatments.^2,42^ Evaluating driver mutations and primary site as both independent and connected variables creates a more nuanced picture of GIST.^39^ Clinical next steps for sites such as the stomach are more established, while protocols for rarer subtypes, like esophageal tumors, are being clarified.^44^
:::

::: {style="border-bottom: 1px solid #ccc; height: 120x; line-height: 23px; text-align: justify; padding: 0 15px; margin-bottom: 10px; font-size: 1rem;"}
**GIST is recognized as a solid-tumor model for precision oncology. Molecular subtype intersects with other disease variables to guide clinical strategy from diagnosis throughout treatment. Evaluating heterogeneity within this sarcoma class offers a more complete picture of each GIST case and of the disease as a whole.**
:::

::: justified-text
Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) present with substantial case-by-case diversity across multiple interrelated factors. Genetic subtype determines which therapies a tumor will most likely respond to at the outset, while age and primary site each offer clues to that subtype and independently shape risk assessment and clinical protocol. Honoring this diversity enables more precise treatment of this rare cancer, and emerging tools like predictive deep learning have the potential to increase that precision by offering a sharper understanding of GIST molecular diversity.
:::
